name: The octave of the Lord (the Circumcision)
what_happens: Mass; in the old rule a fast against the heathen new-year revels.
what_it_means_for_trade: No market. Still inside the twelve days: nobody works.

name: Epiphany (Twelfth Night)
what_happens: The twelve days of Christmas end. The priest gives out the date of Easter (?).
what_it_means_for_trade: Work begins again the next day. From now every port knows when Lent starts and fish will be wanted.

name: Candlemas (the Purification)
what_happens: Candles are blessed and carried in procession.
what_it_means_for_trade: Wax is wanted before it. The time to buy fish for Lent and look the ship over.

name: Light-dues at Candlemas
what_happens: A halfpenny of wax from every hide to the church; again on Easter eve and at All Saints.
what_it_means_for_trade: Wax sells in English ports three times a year.

name: The day Christ overcame the devil
what_happens: A holiday for free men.
what_it_means_for_trade: No hired hands that day.

name: Saint Gregory
what_happens: The pope who sent the faith to the English; a holiday for free men. Falls in Lent.
what_it_means_for_trade: No work; no meat either.

name: Saint Edward the Martyr
what_happens: The king killed at Corfe in 978; his day ordered kept by law.
what_it_means_for_trade: A holiday in English ports in the late game.

name: Lady Day (the Annunciation)
what_happens: Mass. It falls in Lent in most years, so it is kept without meat.
what_it_means_for_trade: Not yet a rent day. No market.
source: V Aethelred 14 (Mary's feasts, with a fast before)

name: The Greater Litany
what_happens: A procession round the fields with relics, and a fast.
what_it_means_for_trade: No meat, no work till the procession is home.

name: Philip and James
what_happens: The one apostles' feast with no fast before it, because it lies in Easter time.
what_it_means_for_trade: A feast with meat: beasts and ale sell.

name: Saint John the Baptist (Midsummer)
what_happens: The great feast of the sailing months, with a fast on its eve. The true longest day is a week past.
what_it_means_for_trade: Every town is full and off its guard. High season begins; the long voyages are under way.

name: Saints Peter and Paul
what_happens: One day of rest in Frankish and English law; the patronal feast of York, Cologne and Nantes, and of Saint Paul's in London.
what_it_means_for_trade: No market that day; a crowd in those four ports the days around it.

name: Saint Martin in summer
what_happens: Martin's ordination and the moving of his body: the summer feast of his churches.
what_it_means_for_trade: A gathering at Utrecht in the months when ships can reach it.

name: Lammas (Saint Peter's Chains)
what_happens: A loaf of the new corn is blessed. The Chronicle dates by it.
what_it_means_for_trade: Harvest has begun: new grain soon, no hands to hire.

name: Rome-penny (Peter's pence)
what_happens: A penny from every hearth for Saint Peter, by his mass day; a heavy fine for holding it back.
what_it_means_for_trade: Pennies are short up country in late July. The silver goes to Rome by Quentovic and the passes.

name: The Assumption of Mary
what_happens: The harvest feast of Mary, with a fast before it.
what_it_means_for_trade: In Wessex the whole week before is free for free men: nobody loads a ship.

name: The Nativity of Mary
what_happens: Mass, a fast before it.
what_it_means_for_trade: Little; the last long voyages are coming home.
source: V Aethelred 14; in the north by about 800 (?)

name: The Exaltation of the Cross
what_happens: Mass. The autumn Ember fast follows. By Vegetius the safe season ends today.
what_it_means_for_trade: From now each crossing is a risk taken knowingly.

name: Michaelmas (Saint Michael)
where: all Christian lands; ordered in Francia in 813
what_happens: The archangel's feast, when the harvest is in.
what_it_means_for_trade: Rents and reckonings. The game's debt of 480 pennies falls due at Dorestad (the game's rule).

name: Rent-pence at Michaelmas
what_happens: The peasant pays ten rent-pence to his lord.
what_it_means_for_trade: Country people sell before it to raise pennies: goods cheap, coin dear.

name: Saint Remigius
what_happens: A feast ordered kept in 813; a day for money rents on Frankish estates (?).
what_it_means_for_trade: Abbeys have coin and sell their spare wine and grain.
source: Council of Mainz 813, c. 36; the rent day from the 9th-century estate books (?)

name: All Saints
what_happens: New in the north about 800; ordered through the Frankish realm in 835. A fast on its eve.
what_it_means_for_trade: The careful are in harbour. In England the tithe of the year's crops and light-dues are owed.
source: Alcuin, letter to Arn 800 (?); Alfred 43; I Cnut 8, 12

name: All Souls
where: the houses of Cluny, then Francia
what_happens: Masses and alms for all the dead.
what_it_means_for_trade: Bread and ale are given at abbey gates.

name: Martinmas (Saint Martin)
what_happens: Winter begins. The beasts that will not be wintered are killed and salted; the new wine is tasted.
what_it_means_for_trade: The sea is shut by the old rule. Salt is dearest just before it; meat and hides cheapest just after. Servants are paid and let go.
source: Council of Mainz 813, c. 36; Vegetius IV.39; ASC 1006, 1009

name: Church-scot at Martinmas
what_happens: Grain owed to the church from every household; sixty shillings and twelve times the due from the man who holds it back. The peasant also owes his lord 23 measures of barley and two hens.
what_it_means_for_trade: Grain moves to the minsters; barley is asked for.

name: Rents in kind at Martinmas
what_happens: The commonest day for rents in pigs, hens and wine on Frankish estates (?).
what_it_means_for_trade: Lords' cellars are full: wine and salt pork are cheap at the abbeys.
source: the estate books of Saint-Germain (about 825) and Pruem (893) (?)

name: Saint Brice's day
what_happens: In 1002 King Aethelred ordered all the Danish men in England killed on this day.
what_it_means_for_trade: 13 November 1002 only: a Dane in an English port is in danger of his life, and so is a crew that looks Danish.

name: Saint Andrew
what_happens: A feast ordered kept in 813. Advent begins on the Sunday nearest it.
what_it_means_for_trade: The Saint-Denis fair is over by now at the latest. The last river barges tie up.

name: Christmas (Midwinter)
what_happens: Four days of rest in Francia, twelve in England, to the Epiphany. Kings hold court, wear their crowns and give gifts. A fast on the eve.
what_it_means_for_trade: No market, no court, no oath, no work. Before it: wine, wax, spices, furs and fine cloth are wanted wherever the king is.
source: Council of Mainz 813, c. 36; Alfred 43; I Cnut 17

name: The emperor's men pay at London
rule: also at Easter
what_happens: The merchants of the emperor's lands, who come in their ships, give at Christmas and at Easter two grey cloths and one brown, ten pounds of pepper, five pairs of gloves and two small casks of vinegar.
what_it_means_for_trade: Rhinelanders are at London on those two feasts with pepper, cloth and wine, and have the right to buy aboard ship.

name: Septuagesima
rule: easter-63
what_happens: The run-up to Lent begins. In England no oaths or ordeals from now until two weeks after Easter.
what_it_means_for_trade: A lawsuit that needs an oath waits eleven weeks.

name: Ash Wednesday: Lent begins
rule: easter-46
what_happens: Forty fast days to Holy Saturday. No flesh of beast or bird; by the strict rule no milk, butter, cheese or eggs. One meal, late in the day. No weddings, no feasting.
what_it_means_for_trade: Herring, stockfish, dried fish, eels and salmon are wanted; meat, cheese and butter do not sell. Ships are being tarred, not sailed.
source: Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae 4; Theodulf, Capitula I.40 (?); Wihtred 14

name: Palm Sunday
rule: easter-7
what_happens: A procession with branches; Holy Week begins. In Wessex the week is free for free men.
what_it_means_for_trade: Nothing is loaded this week in a Christian port.

name: Maundy Thursday
rule: easter-3
what_happens: Penitents are taken back; the holy oils are blessed; lords wash poor men's feet and give alms.
what_it_means_for_trade: Alms are given at every church door. Trier was burned on this day in 882.

name: Good Friday
rule: easter-2
what_happens: The hardest fast of the year: nothing till evening, then bread and water. No mass and no bell.
what_it_means_for_trade: No trade at all.
source: general rule; no single text checked (?)

name: Holy Saturday
rule: easter-1
what_happens: The vigil of Easter and the great day for baptisms, in white clothes.
what_it_means_for_trade: Fine linen and wax are wanted before it. Northmen came into Paris on this day in 845.

name: Easter
rule: easter+0: the Sunday after the first full moon on or after 21 March, by the 19-year table (22 March to 25 April)
what_happens: The year's first feast and a week of rest. The king keeps it at a palace, and the annals say where.
what_it_means_for_trade: Meat, eggs and cheese sell again. Crews are hired and partnerships sworn for the season. Where the king is, his court buys everything.
source: Bede, The Reckoning of Time (725); Council of Mainz 813, c. 36; Alfred 43; ARF

name: Plough-alms
rule: easter+14
what_happens: A penny from every plough to the church.
what_it_means_for_trade: Small; pennies leave the farms.

name: The Rogation days (gang days)
rule: easter+36 to easter+38 (Monday to Wednesday before the Ascension)
what_happens: Processions round the fields with cross and relics; a fast; no work.
what_it_means_for_trade: Three days lost in any Christian port. The first North Sea crossings begin about now.
source: Council of Orleans 511; Clovesho 747, c. 16; ASC (gang days)

name: The Ascension (Holy Thursday)
rule: easter+39
what_happens: A feast of rest in both lists.
what_it_means_for_trade: No market.

name: Pentecost (Whitsun)
rule: easter+49
what_happens: Kept like Easter, with a fast on its eve; the second day for baptisms. Kings hold court and are crowned (Edgar, 973).
what_it_means_for_trade: The sea is open by anybody's rule. In England the tithe of young beasts is due.
source: Council of Mainz 813, c. 36; II Edgar 3; ASC 973

name: Friday fast
rule: every Friday that is not a feast
what_happens: No meat.
what_it_means_for_trade: Fish sells every Thursday. A crew fed meat on a Friday in port is talked about.

name: Ember days of spring
rule: Wednesday, Friday and Saturday of the first week of March (Mainz 813); after 1095, of the first week of Lent
what_happens: A fast; priests are ordained on the Saturday.
what_it_means_for_trade: In Wessex the Wednesday is the slaves' own day to sell what is theirs.
source: Council of Mainz 813, c. 34; W:Ember days; Alfred 43

name: Ember days of summer
rule: Wednesday, Friday and Saturday of the second week of June (Mainz 813); elsewhere the week after Pentecost
what_happens: A fast.
what_it_means_for_trade: Fish in the sailing season; the slaves' Wednesday in Wessex.
source: Council of Mainz 813, c. 34; W:Ember days; Alfred 43

name: Ember days of autumn
rule: Wednesday, Friday and Saturday of the third week of September, after Holy Cross day
what_happens: A fast.
what_it_means_for_trade: The slaves' Wednesday in Wessex; herring is in.
source: Council of Mainz 813, c. 34; W:Ember days; Alfred 43

name: Ember days of winter
rule: Wednesday, Friday and Saturday of the full week before Christmas Eve
what_happens: A fast inside Advent.
what_it_means_for_trade: The slaves' Wednesday in Wessex.
source: Council of Mainz 813, c. 34; W:Ember days; Alfred 43

name: Advent (Saint Martin's Lent)
rule: from Martinmas in the old Gaulish rule, or from the Sunday nearest Saint Andrew, to Christmas Eve
what_happens: A lighter Lent: three days a week by old Gaulish rule; monks keep it whole. In England no oaths or ordeals from Advent to a week after the Epiphany.
what_it_means_for_trade: Fish again; lawsuits wait.

name: Vigil fasts
rule: the day before each feast of Mary and of each apostle (not Philip and James), and before Christmas, Pentecost, Saint John, Saint Laurence and All Saints
what_happens: A fast on the eve; the feast begins at vespers.
what_it_means_for_trade: Meat is bought the day before the eve and eaten the day after.

name: The great fast of 1009
rule: the Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday before Michaelmas 1009
what_happens: With the great army in the land all the people are to fast on bread, herbs and water, go barefoot to church, and give a penny from every hide.
what_it_means_for_trade: Nothing sells but bread and greens. Strangers are watched.
source: VII Aethelred (the day of the month reckoned, not read) (?)

name: Sunday
rule: every week, from Saturday afternoon to dawn on Monday
what_happens: No servile work, no market, no court. In Ireland no journeys either. Among English and Danes a man who trades on Sunday loses the goods and pays twelve ores if a Dane, thirty shillings if English.
what_it_means_for_trade: A day lost in every Christian port; a day gained in a heathen one.
source: Admonitio generalis 81 (789); II Aethelstan 24; Edward and Guthrum 7; I Cnut 14-15; II Edgar 5; Cain Domnaig

name: The Truce of God
rule: every week from Wednesday evening to Monday morning, and through Advent and Lent
where: Francia: the south from 1027, Normandy from 1047, Flanders from 1063
what_happens: Bishops forbid all fighting on those days, on pain of being cut off from the Church.
what_it_means_for_trade: Roads and rivers are a little safer four days in seven.

name: Saint Boniface and his companions
what_happens: Killed at Dokkum on 5 June 754. Pilgrims come by boat to the church and the spring.
what_it_means_for_trade: A crowd at a terp village that is empty the rest of the year.

name: Saint Willibrord
what_happens: The first bishop of the Frisians, died 739. With Martinmas four days later it makes Utrecht's high week.
what_it_means_for_trade: The last gathering before the river trade stops for winter.

name: Saint Lebuin
what_happens: The English priest of the IJssel, died about 775; his church was burned by Saxons and rebuilt by Liudger.
what_it_means_for_trade: The day after Martinmas: one gathering of two feasts at Deventer.

name: Saint Liudger
what_happens: Missionary of the Frisians and first bishop of Muenster, died 809; buried at Werden.
what_it_means_for_trade: Falls in Lent: a mass, not a market.

name: Saint Gregory of Utrecht
what_happens: Abbot of Saint Martin's and master of its school, died about 776.
what_it_means_for_trade: A minor feast of the minster.

name: Saint Radbod of Utrecht
what_happens: Bishop in exile at Deventer, died 917.
what_it_means_for_trade: Little.

name: Saint Bavo
what_happens: The feast of the older abbey at Ghent; a fair grows on it in the 11th century (?).
what_it_means_for_trade: Flemish cloth and wool change hands; before about 1050 only a feast.
source: the feast is old; the fair (?)

name: Saint Amand
what_happens: The missionary who founded both abbeys at Ghent and the first church at Antwerp.
what_it_means_for_trade: A winter feast: local.

name: Saint Gereon
what_happens: First of Cologne's three October feasts (Gereon, the Virgins on the 21st, Severin on the 23rd).
what_it_means_for_trade: The city is full as the vintage comes down the river: wine is cheap, lodging dear.

name: The Holy Virgins of Cologne
what_happens: The martyred virgins; not yet eleven thousand, and not yet Ursula's, before the 10th century.
what_it_means_for_trade: Pilgrims; relics are asked for.

name: Saint Heribert
what_happens: Archbishop of Cologne, died 1021; buried at Deutz across the river.
what_it_means_for_trade: Little; in Lent.

name: Saint Alban of Mainz
what_happens: The feast of the abbey south of the city, rebuilt 787 to 805, where the councils of 813 and 847 met.
what_it_means_for_trade: A summer gathering at Mainz, three days before Saint John. It is also the game's first day.

name: Saint Denis
what_happens: Denis, Rusticus and Eleutherius. The fair opens.
what_it_means_for_trade: See the fair of Saint-Denis.

name: Saint Genevieve
what_happens: The city's own protector; her shrine was carried out against the Northmen in 885.
what_it_means_for_trade: A winter feast: local.

name: Saint Judoc (Josse)
what_happens: A Breton hermit by the Canche. His cell was given to Alcuin in 792 as a guest house for those crossing the sea.
what_it_means_for_trade: Lodging for travellers at Quentovic all year; the feast itself is in the dead season.

name: Saint Audoenus (Ouen)
what_happens: Bishop of Rouen, died about 684; the abbey outside the walls.
what_it_means_for_trade: A harvest-time gathering at Rouen.

name: Saint Romanus
what_happens: Bishop and patron of Rouen. The fair on his day is written of only after 1066 (?).
what_it_means_for_trade: A feast, not yet a fair.

name: Saints Donatian and Rogatian
what_happens: The two brothers martyred at Nantes.
what_it_means_for_trade: A May feast as the salt season opens.

name: Saint Philibert
what_happens: The founder's feast on his island. The monks carried his body to the mainland in 836.
what_it_means_for_trade: To 836 a feast in the salt season with buyers on the island; after it the island is all but empty.

name: Saint Erkenwald
what_happens: Bishop of London, died 693; his body at Saint Paul's.
what_it_means_for_trade: A spring gathering at Saint Paul's as the first ships come up the river.

name: Saint Aelfheah (Alphege)
what_happens: Archbishop killed by drunken Danes at Greenwich in 1012; buried in Saint Paul's, moved to Canterbury by Cnut in 1023.
what_it_means_for_trade: A saint made by Northmen and honoured by a Northman king: a safe thing for a Dane to give alms to.

name: Saint Swithun
rule: also 2 July, the day he died
what_happens: Bishop of Winchester, died about 862; nobody's saint until his body was moved into the minster in 971.
what_it_means_for_trade: From 971 pilgrims go up the Itchen in July.

name: Saint Botolph
what_happens: Founder of the minster at Iken in 654. Later a day for things in Norway (?).
what_it_means_for_trade: A June gathering near Ipswich.

name: Saint Edmund
what_happens: King of the East Angles, killed by the Danes in 869. By about 895 the Danes of East Anglia struck pennies in his name.
what_it_means_for_trade: Saint Edmund pennies pass in East Anglia from about 895 to 915.

name: Saint Felix
what_happens: The first bishop of the East Angles; the see ends about 870.
what_it_means_for_trade: Local; in Lent.

name: Saint Wilfrid
rule: also 24 April
what_happens: Bishop of York, died 709 or 710; buried at Ripon.
what_it_means_for_trade: An autumn feast before York's river grows quiet.

name: Saint John of Beverley
what_happens: Bishop of York, died 721; he ordained Bede.
what_it_means_for_trade: Local.

name: Saint Oswald the king
what_happens: Killed in 642. His uncorrupt right arm lay in a silver box in Saint Peter's church at Bamburgh; his head with Cuthbert.
what_it_means_for_trade: The king's men are at Bamburgh for the feast.

name: Saint Cuthbert
what_happens: The day he died, 687. It falls in Lent.
what_it_means_for_trade: A fast-day feast: fish and wax.

name: Saint Cuthbert in September
what_happens: The moving of his body: the feast that can be kept with meat. The community leaves the island with the body in 875.
what_it_means_for_trade: The gathering on Holy Island, to 875. The tide decides who gets there.
source: Symeon of Durham (late for the wandering) (?)

name: Saint Aidan
what_happens: The Irish founder of Lindisfarne, died at Bamburgh 651.
what_it_means_for_trade: Local.

name: Bede
what_happens: Died on the eve of the Ascension 735. In 793 he is not yet called a saint at Jarrow, only the master.
what_it_means_for_trade: Books: his are asked for from here to Mainz.
source: Cuthbert's letter on the death of Bede

name: Saint Hild
what_happens: Abbess of the house on the cliff, died 680. The house ends with the Danes about 867 (?).
what_it_means_for_trade: Local; after Martinmas, so reached only along the coast.

name: Saint Mildrith
what_happens: Abbess of Minster in Thanet, which held toll rights on its ships by the kings' charters.
what_it_means_for_trade: The abbey's ships are toll-free at Sarre and London (?): a July feast on the Wantsum.

name: Saint Augustine of Canterbury
what_happens: The first archbishop; his abbey outside Canterbury's wall.
what_it_means_for_trade: Canterbury's landing is busy.

name: Saint Dunstan
what_happens: Archbishop, died 988; his day ordered kept by Cnut.
what_it_means_for_trade: A holiday in English ports in the late game.

name: Saint Werburgh
what_happens: A Mercian king's daughter; her body was brought to Chester for safety about 875 or 907 (?).
what_it_means_for_trade: Local.

name: Saint Columba (Colum Cille)
what_happens: Died on Iona in 597. The day after the Lindisfarne raid in the calendar.
what_it_means_for_trade: Boats from all the western sea come to Iona, to about 825; after that the relics are at Kells and Dunkeld.

name: Saint Patrick
what_happens: The feast of Armagh's saint, in Lent.
what_it_means_for_trade: Little for a ship: the sea is hardly open.

name: Saint Anskar
what_happens: Archbishop of Hamburg and Bremen, died 3 February 865. He built the churches at Hedeby (about 850) and Ribe (about 860).
what_it_means_for_trade: Christian merchants have a church and a bell at both towns from then; the towns themselves stay mostly heathen for a century.

name: Saint Olaf
what_happens: King Olaf fell at Stiklestad in 1030; his body was taken up and held holy on 3 August 1031.
what_it_means_for_trade: The first saint of the whole northern trade: within a lifetime he has churches in York, London, Dublin and Novgorod. An oath by him is taken everywhere.
source: ASC 1030; Sigvat; Adam of Bremen II.61

name: The fair of Saint-Denis
what_happens: The great autumn fair by the abbey, from Saint Denis's day for four weeks (one account: seven, to Saint Andrew). English and Frisian merchants come for the year's wine, honey and madder, and bring wool cloth.
what_it_means_for_trade: Wine cheap and plenty; cloth sells. The last voyage of the year: up the Seine and home before Martinmas. Tolls belong to the abbey.
source: judgment of 710; charters of 753 and 775; fairs_793.json; dossiers/parisius.md

name: Saint Matthias's fair at Saint-Denis
what_happens: A second, small fair on the day the abbey church was hallowed.
what_it_means_for_trade: A winter market for river boats only. When it began is not known.

name: The Lendit
what_happens: A June fair on the plain between Paris and Saint-Denis, to Saint John.
what_it_means_for_trade: A summer fair for the last years of the game only.

name: The summer market at Ripa
what_happens: The plots by the river fill with bead-makers, comb-makers and Frisian ships.
what_it_means_for_trade: The time to bring Rhenish goods and take amber, hides and combs.

name: The summer market at Skiringssal
what_happens: Vestfold's market: soapstone, whetstones, iron, furs from the north.
what_it_means_for_trade: Open in summer; lived in all year from about 805 (?), gone by 960.

name: The summer market at Birka
what_happens: Ships reach the island once the lake ice has gone.
what_it_means_for_trade: Furs, iron, dirhams; cloth, wine and glass wanted.

name: The market at Sliesthorp
what_happens: The crossing between the two seas in its season.
what_it_means_for_trade: Baltic goods meet North Sea goods; the king's toll from 808.

name: The winter fur market on the ice
what_happens: Winter furs come in by sledge and ski over the frozen lake.
what_it_means_for_trade: No ship can come: only a merchant who winters there buys the best furs at the first price.
source: the Birka finds (ice nails, skates); no text (?)

name: The fair of Tailtiu
what_happens: The king of Tara's assembly at Lughnasa: games, horse racing, law, buying and selling. The annals note the years it failed (disturbed 811, not held 873).
what_it_means_for_trade: Inland, a day's ride from the Liffey: Dublin sells to it and buys from it. A year without it means war in Meath.

name: The Franks' general assembly
rule: where the king calls it, between May and August
what_happens: The great men come with their gifts to the king before the summer's campaign; law is given out. Moved from March to May in 755.
what_it_means_for_trade: A court eats a district bare and pays for wine, wax, spices, furs, horses and arms. The counts are away from their own ports.
source: Hincmar, De ordine palatii 29-30; ARF; Fredegar's continuator 755 (?)

name: The king's Easter and Christmas
rule: Easter and 25 December, at the palace the annals name each year
what_happens: The king keeps the feast at a palace: Aachen most often; Nijmegen in 806 and 808.
what_it_means_for_trade: When it is Nijmegen, the whole delta sells to the court.

name: The count's court
rule: two or three general sittings a year: about summer, about autumn (and in spring)
what_happens: Free men must come. Debts, thefts and land are judged. Not on a Sunday or a feast.
what_it_means_for_trade: The place to claim a debt or answer for one.

name: The hundred court
rule: every four weeks
what_happens: The local court; the borough court sits three times a year and the shire court twice.
what_it_means_for_trade: A claim can be heard within a month, outside the closed seasons for oaths.

name: The folk-moot under the king's reeve
rule: when the reeve holds it
what_happens: Merchants must bring before the king's reeve at the folk-moot the men they mean to take up country, and answer for them.
what_it_means_for_trade: Before going inland from an English port, a master shows his crew to the reeve.

name: The thing at Birka
rule: when the king calls it
what_happens: The townsmen meet in the open. In 852 the king put Anskar's asking to the lots, then to this thing and to a second elsewhere; an old man spoke for the Christians' god, since the way to Dorestad had grown dangerous.
what_it_means_for_trade: The thing gives or refuses a stranger's faith and his peace. A known guest speaks through his host.

name: The Gutnalthing
rule: yearly, at Roma in the middle of the island; the day is not known
what_happens: The island's own assembly, with no king over it.
what_it_means_for_trade: A foreign merchant's peace on Gotland is the thing's to give.

name: The Norwegian law-things
rule: in summer; about Saint Botolph's day in the written laws (?)
what_happens: The Gulathing in the west and the Frostathing in the north: free men's delegates, law said from memory.
what_it_means_for_trade: The great farmers are away for a fortnight; debts are claimed there.
source: Gulathing and Frostathing laws, 12th century and later (?)

name: The Danes' king-taking at Viborg
rule: when a king dies
what_happens: A new king is taken at the thing at Viborg, then at Ringsted and Lund (?). Magnus in 1042.
what_it_means_for_trade: Between kings the king's peace in the markets is in doubt.

name: The Althing of Iceland
rule: the Thursday after nine weeks of summer (about 18 to 24 June by the Julian count (?)); from 999 a week later
what_happens: All Iceland's chieftains meet for two weeks at midsummer.
what_it_means_for_trade: Iceland ships sail for Norway and Dublin after it: wadmal and falcons arrive in late summer.

name: The assembly of the Liutizi at Rethra
rule: when war or peace must be chosen
what_happens: All must agree; one who holds out is beaten, or his goods are burnt. The banners are kept in the temple of Riedegost.
what_it_means_for_trade: A Wendish peace holds for everyone or for nobody. Reric itself is gone after 808; this is the hinterland's rule.

name: Yule (midwinter)
rule: three nights from midwinter night; by some reckonings mid January (?); moved to 25 December in Norway about 950
what_happens: Ale is brewed and Yule is drunk; beasts are killed and eaten; cups for a good year and peace. That Yule was drunk is in a poem of about 900; the rest is told in the 13th century.
what_it_means_for_trade: Nobody travels. Malt and honey are wanted in autumn for the brewing. A guest at a Yule table is offered horse.
source: Haraldskvaedi (about 900); Snorri, Saga of Hakon the Good 13-14 (late); W:Yule

name: Mothers' night
what_happens: Bede says the heathen English began their year on this night and called it Modranecht. By 793 nobody keeps it; the month names (Giuli, Blotmonath) are still used.
what_it_means_for_trade: None. A thing an old monk can tell.
source: Bede, The Reckoning of Time 15 (725); W:Yule

name: Blood month
rule: the month of November
where: England (the name); the whole north (the slaughter)
what_happens: Bede: Blotmonath, when the cattle to be killed were given to the gods. The killing goes on under Saint Martin's name.
what_it_means_for_trade: Salt wanted in October; meat, hides, horn and tallow cheap in November.

name: Winter Nights
rule: three nights from the Saturday between 11 and 17 October (?)
what_happens: Winter begins. The autumn feast after the slaughter, for a good year; the sacrifice to the disir is set here in the western sagas.
what_it_means_for_trade: The Northmen are home and their markets are empty. Hire and leases run from here to the start of summer.
source: Snorri, Ynglinga saga 8; the Icelandic calendar (Ari 4); peoples/norse.md

name: The elves' sacrifice
rule: an evening in autumn, farm by farm
what_happens: A household feast behind shut doors. A Christian poet riding east about 1019 was turned away from farm after farm.
what_it_means_for_trade: No lodging and no dealing that night: a stranger sleeps in his boat.

name: The Disting
rule: in the month of Goi, late February or early March; later rule of thumb: the full of the first moon born after the Epiphany (?)
what_happens: The Svear's chief sacrifice, for peace and the king's victory, with all their things and a market for a week. After the faith came the market was moved to Candlemas and lasts three days.
what_it_means_for_trade: The one great market reached by sledge, not ship: furs, iron and winter goods. A merchant must have wintered in Svealand to be there.
source: Snorri, Saga of Saint Olaf 77 (about 1230); W:Disting; W:Disablot; the Uppland law 1296 (?)

name: The ninth-year feast at Uppsala
rule: every ninth year, about the spring equinox, for nine days; which years is not recorded
what_happens: A common feast of all the Svear. Nine males of every living kind are offered and hung in the grove. Nobody is excused; Christians buy themselves off.
what_it_means_for_trade: A Christian in Svealand that spring pays to stay away. Told as rumour in Christian ports.
source: Adam of Bremen IV.26-27 and its note (about 1075, second hand); W:Blot

name: The ninth-year feast at Lejre
rule: every ninth year in January, after the Epiphany; which years is not recorded
what_happens: All gather at the kings' seat; ninety-nine men and as many horses are offered, with dogs and cocks. Said to have ended in 934.
what_it_means_for_trade: Midwinter: no ship is there to see it. A thing told of the Danes in Saxon and Frankish ports.
source: Thietmar I.17 (1012 to 1018, second hand); W:Blot

name: The sacrifice for victory
rule: at the start of summer, the Thursday between 9 and 15 April (?)
what_happens: The third of the three yearly sacrifices, before the ships go out.
what_it_means_for_trade: The season opens: crews gather, raiders with them. A fortnight later their sails may be seen.

name: The town's feast at Hedeby
rule: day not known
what_happens: The people gather to honour their god with eating and drinking. A man who kills a beast hangs it on a pole before his door, so that all know he has made his offering.
what_it_means_for_trade: Beasts sell before it. A Christian guest must choose whether to eat.

name: Lots before a voyage
rule: before any great choice
what_happens: Lots are cast to learn which god will help and whether the venture will go well.
what_it_means_for_trade: A northern partner may not sail, or not that week, because the lots said no.

name: The first signing
rule: any day; no feast
where: the Norse lands and their markets
what_happens: A heathen takes the sign of the cross without baptism, so that he may eat and deal with Christians and still keep his own gods.
what_it_means_for_trade: A signed Northman can be a Christian's partner and sit at his table.
source: Rimbert, Life of Anskar 24; Egils saga 50 (late)

name: Imbolc (Saint Brigid)
what_happens: Spring begins; the ewes come into milk. Brigid of Kildare's feast.
what_it_means_for_trade: None by sea; a quarter of the Irish year turns.

name: Beltaine
what_happens: Summer begins; cattle are driven between two fires and out to the summer grazing. One of the two hinges of the year for rent and hire.
what_it_means_for_trade: The fighting and sailing season opens in the Irish sea.

name: Lughnasa
what_happens: The first of the harvest; the kings' assemblies and fairs.
what_it_means_for_trade: See the fair of Tailtiu.

name: Samain
what_happens: Winter begins; cattle come home, the beasts not to be wintered are killed, rents and tribute go to the king.
what_it_means_for_trade: Hides and salt meat at Dublin; the end of the season in the Irish sea.

name: Tithe of young beasts
rule: easter+49 (Pentecost)
what_happens: A tenth of the year's young stock to the church.
what_it_means_for_trade: Lambs and calves move to the minsters.

name: Tithe of the earth's fruits
rule: by the equinox (Edgar), by All Saints (Cnut)
what_happens: A tenth of the harvest to the church.
what_it_means_for_trade: Minsters have grain to sell through the winter.

name: The peasant's Easter lamb
rule: easter+0
what_happens: A young sheep or two pence to the lord.
what_it_means_for_trade: A sheep is worth two pence up country at Easter.

name: The sea opens (the old rule)
what_happens: From 10 March to 26 May sailing is possible but doubtful.
what_it_means_for_trade: Short runs and river work; the bold get the first prices.

name: The safe season
what_happens: From 27 May to 14 September the sea is held safe.
what_it_means_for_trade: The long voyages: the Baltic, Norway, the Loire. The raiders' season too.

name: The doubtful autumn
what_happens: From 15 September to 10 November sailing is doubtful: equinox gales, long nights.
what_it_means_for_trade: Home runs, the Saint-Denis fair, the herring. Each crossing is a risk priced in.
source: Vegetius IV.39; ASC 1066 (William's crossing, 27 to 28 September)

name: The sea is shut
what_happens: From Martinmas to 10 March the seas are shut. Boats are hauled up, tarred and left. Armies go into winter quarters about Martinmas.
what_it_means_for_trade: Prices of everything a ship brings climb till spring. News stops: what is known at Martinmas is all that is known till Easter.

name: The northern season
rule: from the start of April to the start of October (?)
what_happens: A Norwegian father's advice to a merchant son: not out before April, not at sea after early October; tar the ship in autumn; settle with your partners before sailing.
what_it_means_for_trade: The north's own rule is shorter in autumn than the Roman one.
source: The King's Mirror, about 1250 (the dates from memory) (?)

name: Ice on the Malar bay
rule: about December to April (a guess at the months)
what_happens: The bay freezes. No ship reaches Birka; sledges do.
what_it_means_for_trade: A ship caught there winters there.

name: Ice on Ladoga and the Volkhov
rule: November to late April or May
what_happens: Lake and river are frozen. The Rus go round their tribute lands in winter and come back to the rivers when the ice melts in April.
what_it_means_for_trade: Furs are gathered in winter and sold in May and June. The year allows one voyage there and back.
source: Constantine Porphyrogenitus, De administrando imperio 9 (about 950, for Kiev); trade_year_793.json

name: Winter quarters
rule: about Martinmas, to spring
what_happens: From 851 in England and the 840s in Francia the heathen hosts no longer go home for winter: they sit on an island or a river mouth.
what_it_means_for_trade: A host in winter quarters makes a market: they buy food and horses and sell captives and plunder. It is also the worst neighbour a port can have.

name: Feast days draw raiders
rule: any great feast in the sailing months
what_happens: A town at a feast is full of people and silver, with its men in church: Nantes on Saint John's day 843, Paris on Holy Saturday 845, Trier on Maundy Thursday 882, Chippenham after Twelfth Night 878.
what_it_means_for_trade: A rumour of sails before a feast is worth acting on: sell and leave, or stay for the feast-day prices.
source: Annals of Angouleme 843; Annals of Saint-Bertin 845; Annals of Fulda 882; ASC 878

name: The funeral ale of the Ests
rule: when a man of means dies: a month or two, for a king up to half a year
what_happens: The dead man lies unburnt in his house while kin and friends drink and play; on the day of the burning what is left of his goods is laid out in heaps along a mile and raced for on horseback. They know how to make cold, so the dead do not rot.
what_it_means_for_trade: No fixed day: the one dated-by-custom gathering known for Truso. Mead and ale are drunk in quantity; fast horses are dear.
source: Wulfstan, in the Old English Orosius (about 890)
